intro: A kitchen is full of things that can hurt you. A stove that looks cool. A pot of steam. A pair of scissors. A glass that breaks. Most of them do not look dangerous at all. That is the tricky part.

In this unit you learn two big rules. Hot has no color, so ask before you touch. Sharp things travel point-down, so carry and pass them the right way. You will also learn what to do for a small burn and when a job belongs to a grown-up.
By the end, you will know how to stay safe near a stove, an oven, a freezer and a drawer of tools. You will be a helper a grown-up can trust in the kitchen.
bigQuestion: How do we stay safe around things that are hot, cold and sharp?

timeline.t: Walk into the kitchen. Stop and look. What is on the stove? What is on the table?
See a mug or a pan. Ask a grown-up: Is this hot? Wait for the answer.
A grown-up lifts a lid. Step back. Let the steam go up, not at you.
A tray comes out of the oven. A grown-up wears a dry mitt. You stay back.
Check the pot handles. They point in, toward the back of the stove.
Time to help cut. Get the butter knife and the cutting board. Curl your fingers.
Pass the scissors handle first. Say Got it? Wait. Then let go.
Something falls. Step back. Let it land. Tell a grown-up.
A small burn? Cool running water for a long time. Then tell a grown-up.
Put every tool back, point down, in its place. The kitchen is safe again.

words.d: so warm it can hurt your skin; you cannot see it
hot water floating in the air; it can burn you
a thick glove that keeps hot things from burning your hand
the part of a pot or tool you hold; on a pot it turns in
the very cold box kept at 0 °F; cold can hurt too
a hurt spot from something hot; cool water and tell a grown-up
a thing with a job, like a knife or scissors; not a toy
the sharp tip of a tool; it always travels down

test.q: Why do you ask before touching a pan?
test.why: You cannot see heat. Asking a grown-up is the only sure way.

test.q: What comes out of a pot when the lid is lifted?
test.why: Steam rushes out when a lid comes off. It can burn.

test.q: Which is the right tool for a hot tray?
test.why: A dry mitt blocks heat. Wet cloth lets heat through fast.

test.q: Which way do pot handles point?
choices: Toward the back of the stove
test.why: Handles turned in cannot be bumped and tipped.

test.q: You get a small burn. First step?
test.why: Cool water takes heat out of the skin. Then tell a grown-up.

test.q: How cold is a freezer kept?
test.why: Freezers are kept at 0 °F. Fridges are at or below 40 °F.
Closed and point down means a trip cannot hurt anyone.

test.q: How do you pass a sharp tool?
test.why: Handle first keeps every hand away from the point and edge.

test.q: A knife falls off the counter. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
test.why: Never catch a falling knife. The floor can take the hit.

test.q: Which job is for a grown-up only?
choices: Cutting a banana with a butter knife
test.why: Matches and lighters make fire. They are off-limits for kids.

write.prompt: Draw or write a safety plan for helping in the kitchen. List five steps you follow. For each step, say what you do and why it keeps you safe.
tips: Put the steps in order, from walking in to putting tools away.
Name the tool for each step: mitt, butter knife, cutting board.
Say the rule: hot has no color, or point down.
Say what you do if something goes wrong, like a burn or a fall.

title: Hot, Cold and Sharp

chapters.title: Hot Has No Color
chapters.bigQuestion: How can you tell if something is hot when hot has no color?

story.title: The Cocoa That Looked Cool
story.kicker: A mug on the table looks safe. It is not.
paragraphs: Mia came into the kitchen after school. A blue mug sat on the table. It did not steam. It did not glow. It just looked like a mug of cocoa, ready to drink.
Mia grabbed the mug with both hands. Ouch! It was hot. She let go fast. The cocoa sloshed onto the table. Her fingers stung.
Dad ran cool water over her fingers. He held them under the tap for a long time. Then he said, "Hot has no color, Mia. You cannot see hot. You have to ask."
The next day Mia saw a mug on the table again. This time she did not touch it. She asked first. "Is this hot?" Dad smiled. "Good question. Yes, it is."
story.think: Why could Mia not tell the mug was hot just by looking at it?

lessons.title: Ask Before You Touch
lessons.mainIdea: Hot has no color, so ask a grown-up before you touch anything in the kitchen.
reading: Look at a stove *burner* that is turned off. Now picture it turned on low. It looks the same. It is not the same. One can burn your hand.
A pan handle looks cool. A mug looks cool. A plate from the oven looks cool. Hot has no color. Your eyes cannot see it.
So here is the rule. Ask a grown-up first. Say, "Is this hot?" Wait for the answer. Then decide.

words.d: the round part on top of a stove that gets hot
so warm it can hurt your skin

look.title: Two Mugs on a Table
look.text: Look at the two red mugs on the table. They look the same. One came from the cupboard. One came from the microwave just now. Nothing steams. Nothing glows.
look.prompt: Which mug is hot? How could you find out without touching?

check.q: A stove burner is turned on low. What does it look like?
choices: It looks the same as when it is off
check.why: Hot has no color. A warm burner can look just like a cold one.

check.q: You see a mug on the table. What should you do first?
choices: Ask a grown-up if it is hot
check.why: Asking first keeps your hands safe. You cannot see hot.

check.q: Why can you not tell a pan is hot by looking?
check.why: Heat does not change how most things look. Your eyes cannot see it.

lessons.title: Steam Is Hot Too
lessons.mainIdea: Steam is hot water in the air, and it can burn just like a hot pan.
reading: A pot of soup bubbles on the stove. White puffs rise from the top. That is *steam*. Steam is water that got so hot it floats.
Steam can burn you. It is hotter than bath water. When a grown-up lifts a lid, steam rushes out. Keep your face and hands back.
The same is true for a microwave. Open a bowl of soup slowly. Tip the lid away from your face. Let the steam go up, not at you.

words.d: hot water floating in the air; it can burn you

look.title: Lifting the Lid
look.text: A grown-up is about to lift the lid off a pot of noodles. You are standing right next to the stove. Your face is close to the pot. Picture what will come out when the lid comes up.
look.prompt: Where should you stand before the lid comes off? Why?

check.q: What is steam?
choices: Very hot water in the air
check.why: Steam is water that got so hot it floats up. It can burn.

check.q: A grown-up lifts a lid off a hot pot. What should you do?
choices: Put your face over the pot to smell it
Keep your face and hands back
check.why: Steam rushes out when a lid comes off. Stay back from it.

check.q: You open a hot bowl from the microwave. How?
choices: With your nose over the bowl
Slowly, with the lid tipped away from you
check.why: Tipping the lid away lets steam go up and not at your face.

lessons.title: Mitts and Pot Holders
lessons.mainIdea: An oven mitt or pot holder goes between your hand and anything hot.
reading: A tray of muffins is ready. The oven is at 350 °F. That is very hot. Nobody touches the tray with a bare hand.
A grown-up puts on an oven *mitt*. A mitt is a thick glove. It goes between your hand and the hot tray. A *pot holder* is a thick square. It works the same way.
Never use a wet towel. Water lets heat through fast. A wet towel can burn you. Use a dry mitt every time.

words.d: a thick glove that keeps hot things from burning your hand
a thick square of cloth for holding a hot pan

look.title: What Goes on the Hand?
look.text: On the counter you see three things: a dry oven mitt, a wet dish towel, and a paper napkin. A hot pan of rolls needs to come out of the oven right now.
look.prompt: Which one should the grown-up put on? What is wrong with the other two?

check.q: What does an oven mitt do?
choices: It keeps heat from your hand
check.why: A mitt is thick. It sits between your hand and the hot pan.

check.q: Why is a wet towel a bad pot holder?
check.why: Wet cloth carries heat to your skin quickly. Use a dry mitt.

check.q: The oven is set to 350 °F. Who takes the tray out?
choices: A grown-up with a dry mitt
check.why: Oven jobs are grown-up jobs at this age, and a dry mitt is the safe tool.

lessons.title: Handles Turned In
lessons.mainIdea: Pot handles point in toward the back of the stove so nobody can bump them.
reading: Picture a pot on the front burner. Its handle sticks out over the edge. A little brother walks by. His arm hits the handle. The hot pot tips.
Now picture the same pot. The *handle* is turned in. It points toward the wall. Nobody can bump it. Nothing tips.
That is the rule. Handles turn in. Use the back burners when you can. Never grab a handle. It might be hot too.

words.d: the long part of a pot or pan that you hold

look.title: Fix the Stove
look.text: Look at the stove. Two pots are cooking. One pot's handle sticks straight out over the front edge of the stove. The other pot's handle points at the wall. A dog and a toddler are in the kitchen.
look.prompt: Which pot is safe? What should a grown-up do about the other one?

check.q: Which way should a pot handle point?
choices: In, toward the back of the stove
check.why: A handle turned in cannot be bumped, so the pot cannot tip.

check.q: A handle sticks out over the front. What could happen?
choices: Someone bumps it and the pot tips
check.why: A handle that sticks out is easy to hit. A hot pot could fall.

check.q: Which burner is safest for a pot?
choices: The one closest to the front
The one with the biggest flame
check.why: Back burners are farther from little hands and walking bodies.

lessons.title: Cold Can Hurt Too
lessons.mainIdea: Very cold things like ice and freezer shelves can hurt your skin, so hold them briefly.
reading: Open the *freezer*. The freezer is kept at 0 °F. That is much colder than a fridge. Your breath makes a cloud.
Hold an ice cube in your bare hand. First it feels cool. Then it stings. Then it hurts. Very cold can hurt like hot.
So do not hold ice for a long time. Do not touch metal in the freezer with wet hands. Ask a grown-up to get frozen food out.

words.d: the very cold box that keeps food frozen hard

look.title: How Cold, How Hot
look.cite: USDA food-safety temperatures for fridge and freezer; oven and bath are typical examples
look.prompt: Which number is the coldest? Which could burn you?

check.q: You hold an ice cube for a long time. What happens?
choices: It starts to sting and hurt
check.why: Very cold hurts skin, just as very hot does. Hold ice only briefly.

check.q: How cold is a freezer kept?
check.why: A freezer is kept at 0 °F. That is cold enough to hurt bare skin.

check.q: Who should get frozen food out of the freezer?
check.why: Frozen food and cold metal can hurt. Ask a grown-up to help.

lessons.title: A Small Burn: Cool Water
lessons.mainIdea: For a small burn, run cool water on it and tell a grown-up right away.
reading: Say you touch a hot pan. Your finger stings. Here is what to do. First, go to the sink. Run *cool water* over the burn.
Keep it under the water. Count slowly. Keep going for a long time. Cool water takes the heat out of your skin.
Then tell a grown-up. Always tell. Do not put butter or ice on a burn. Those make it worse. Cool water and a grown-up are the answer.

words.d: water from the tap that is not hot and not icy
a hurt spot on your skin from something hot

look.title: Steps in Order
look.text: Here are the steps for a small burn, but they are mixed up: Tell a grown-up. Touch a hot pan by mistake. Keep the burn under the water for a long time. Go to the sink and run cool water on it.
look.prompt: Put the steps in the right order. Say them out loud.

check.q: You get a small burn. What is the first thing to do?
check.why: Cool running water takes heat out of the skin. It is the first step.

check.q: What should you NOT put on a burn?
check.why: Ice and butter make a burn worse. Use cool water only.

check.q: After the cool water, what do you do?
check.why: A grown-up needs to see every burn. Always tell.

review.q: Why should you ask before you touch a pan?
review.why: You cannot see heat. Asking a grown-up is the only sure way.

review.q: What comes out when a lid is lifted off a hot pot?
review.why: Steam rushes out when a lid comes off. It can burn.

review.q: Which is the safe tool for a hot tray?
review.why: A dry mitt blocks heat. Wet cloth lets heat through.

review.q: Where should a pot handle point?
choices: Toward the back of the stove
review.why: Handles turned in cannot be bumped by a passing arm.

review.q: What temperature is a freezer kept at?
review.why: Freezers are kept at 0 °F. Fridges are at or below 40 °F.

review.q: You burn your finger. What are the two right steps?
choices: Cool water, then tell a grown-up
review.why: Cool running water first, then always tell a grown-up.

chapters.title: Sharp Things Travel Point-Down
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we use sharp tools so nobody gets hurt?

story.title: Passing the Scissors
story.kicker: One pair of scissors, six kids, and one right way to pass them.
paragraphs: It was craft time. Six kids sat at one table. There was one pair of scissors. Leo had them. Ava needed them next. "Toss them here!" she said.
Leo lifted the scissors to throw. Ms. Ruiz said, "Stop." She walked over. "Scissors are a tool. Tools never fly. Close them. Hold the blades. Hand over the handles."
Leo closed the scissors. He held the closed blades in his fist. He turned the handles toward Ava. She took the handles. Nobody's fingers were near a point.
"That is how we pass sharp things," said Ms. Ruiz. "Handle first. Point down. Every time." The whole table tried it. Slowly, the scissors went all the way around.
story.think: What could have happened if Leo had tossed the scissors to Ava?

lessons.title: A Tool Has a Job
lessons.mainIdea: Knives, scissors and forks are tools with a job, and tools are never toys.
reading: Look in a kitchen drawer. A knife. A fork. A pair of scissors. Each one is a *tool*. A tool has a job. A knife cuts. A fork lifts food. Scissors cut paper.
A tool is not a toy. You do not swing it. You do not poke with it. You do not run with it. When the job is done, the tool goes back.
The *point* is the sharp tip. The *edge* is the sharp side. Keep your fingers away from both. Then the tool can only do its job.

words.d: a thing that helps you do a job, like a knife or scissors
the sharp tip of a tool
the sharp side of a knife or scissor blade

look.title: Toy or Tool?
look.text: Look at the things on the rug: a stuffed bear, a fork, a rubber ball, a pair of scissors, a wooden block, a butter knife. Some belong in the toy bin. Some belong in the kitchen drawer.
look.prompt: Sort them. Which ones are tools? What is each tool's job?

check.q: What is a knife?
check.why: A knife is a tool. Its job is to cut. Tools are never toys.

check.q: Which part of a knife is the sharp tip?
check.why: The point is the sharp tip. The edge is the sharp side.

check.q: A kid swings scissors like a sword. What is wrong?
choices: Scissors are too heavy to swing
Scissors are a tool, not a toy
check.why: Swinging a sharp tool can cut someone. Tools do only their job.

lessons.title: Closed and Pointed Down
lessons.mainIdea: Carry scissors closed, in your fist, with the point down, and walk.
reading: You need to take scissors across the room. Here is how. First, close them. Then wrap your fist around the closed *blades*. The point faces the floor.
Now walk. Never run. If you trip, the point goes at the floor. Not at you. Not at a friend.
A grown-up carries a knife the same way. Point down. Edge away from the body. Walking, not running.

words.d: the two sharp parts of scissors that do the cutting

look.title: Three Kids Walking
look.text: Look at three kids crossing the classroom with scissors. Sam runs with the scissors open and pointed up. Jo walks with the scissors closed, in her fist, point down. Ken walks holding the scissors by one handle, blades swinging.
look.prompt: Who is carrying the scissors the right way? What should the other two change?

check.q: How do you carry scissors?
choices: Closed, in your fist, point down
check.why: Closed and point down means a trip cannot hurt you or a friend.

check.q: Why do you walk, not run, with scissors?
choices: If you trip, the point could hurt someone
check.why: A fall with a sharp tool is the danger. Walking makes a fall less likely.

check.q: A grown-up carries a knife. Which way does the point go?
check.why: Point down, edge away from the body, walking. Same rule as scissors.

lessons.title: Handle First
lessons.mainIdea: Hand a sharp tool to someone handle-first so their hand never touches the sharp part.
reading: A friend asks for the scissors. Do not toss them. Close them. Hold the blades. Turn the *handle* toward your friend.
Your friend takes the handle. Say, "Got it?" Wait for "Got it." Then let go. Now nobody's hand was near the point.
Grown-ups pass knives the same way. Or they set the knife down. Then the other person picks it up. Either way, no hand meets an edge.

words.d: the part of a tool you hold; it is not sharp

look.title: Pass It Right
look.text: Here are the steps for passing scissors, mixed up: Let go. Close the scissors. Say Got it? and wait for the answer. Hold the closed blades and turn the handle toward your friend.
look.prompt: Put the steps in order. Then practice with a pencil, point down.

check.q: Which part of the scissors do you hand to your friend?
check.why: Handle first means your friend's hand never touches the sharp part.

check.q: When do you let go of the scissors?
choices: After your friend says Got it
check.why: Waiting for Got it means the scissors are not dropped between you.

check.q: A friend across the table asks for scissors. What do you do?
check.why: Sharp tools never fly. Walk them over and pass the handle.

lessons.title: Let It Fall
lessons.mainIdea: Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and let it fall.
reading: A knife slips off the counter. Your hands want to grab it. Do not. Step back. Let it *fall*. A knife on the floor hurts nobody.
If you grab, you might catch the edge. That is how hands get cut. The floor can take the hit. Your hand cannot.
After it lands, tell a grown-up. The grown-up picks it up by the handle. Then it gets washed. Then it goes back in the drawer.

words.d: to drop down to the floor

look.title: The Slipping Knife
look.text: Picture a butter knife sliding off the edge of the table in slow motion. Your hand is right there. You could grab it. Or you could step back and let it clatter on the floor.
look.prompt: Which choice keeps your fingers safe? What do you do after it lands?

check.q: A knife falls off the counter. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Grabbing a falling knife can catch the edge. The floor can take the hit.

check.q: Why not catch a falling knife?
choices: You might grab the sharp edge
check.why: A hand that grabs for a knife often finds the edge. Let it fall.

check.q: Who picks the knife up off the floor?
check.why: Picking up a knife is a grown-up job. They hold the handle only.

lessons.title: Butter Knife and Board
lessons.mainIdea: Kids can cut soft food with a butter knife on a cutting board, with a grown-up nearby.
reading: A grown-up says you can help cut a banana. Here is your kit. A *butter knife*. A *cutting board*. The banana. A butter knife has no point. Its edge is dull.
Put the board on the table. Put the banana on the board. Hold the banana with one hand. Curl your fingers in like a claw. Cut with the other hand, slow.
Only soft foods. Banana, cheese, cooked carrots. Only with a grown-up close by. Never a sharp knife. That is a grown-up tool.

words.d: a dull knife with no point; safe for spreading and cutting soft food
a flat board you cut food on so the table stays safe

look.title: Set Up to Cut
look.text: Look at the table. A banana sits on a cutting board. Next to it are a butter knife, a big sharp chef's knife, and a spoon. A grown-up is standing right there. You get to help.
look.prompt: Which knife do you pick up? Where do your fingers go on the banana?

check.q: Which knife is for kids to cut a banana?
check.why: A butter knife is dull with no point. Sharp knives are grown-up tools.

check.q: How do you hold the banana while cutting?
choices: With fingers curled in like a claw
check.why: Curled fingers keep fingertips away from the edge.

check.q: Where does the banana go?
check.why: A cutting board keeps food steady and the table safe.

lessons.title: Grown-Up Jobs
lessons.mainIdea: Broken glass, matches and lighters are for grown-ups only; you tell, you do not touch.
reading: A glass falls and breaks. Stop. Do not pick up the pieces. Do not walk on them. Say, "A glass broke!" A grown-up sweeps it up. Broken glass is a grown-up job.
You find *matches* or a *lighter* on a shelf. Do not touch them. They make fire. Tell a grown-up where they are. That is your whole job.
Tools have jobs. So do people. Some jobs are for kids. Some are only for grown-ups. Knowing which is which keeps you safe.

words.d: small sticks that make fire when struck; grown-ups only
a small tool that makes a flame; grown-ups only

look.title: Whose Job?
look.text: Look at this list of jobs: cut a banana with a butter knife, sweep up a broken glass, put away the scissors, light a candle with a match, carry a sharp knife to the sink, put a fork in the drawer.
look.prompt: Which jobs are for you? Which are for a grown-up only?

check.q: A glass breaks on the floor. What do you do?
choices: Say A glass broke and stay back
check.why: Broken glass cuts. Tell a grown-up and keep away from the pieces.

check.q: You find a lighter on a shelf. What do you do?
choices: Tell a grown-up where it is
check.why: Matches and lighters make fire. Telling a grown-up is your only job.

check.q: Which job is for a kid?
choices: Putting a fork in the drawer
check.why: A fork can be put away by a kid. Fire and glass are grown-up jobs.

review.why: Scissors are a tool. Their job is cutting. Tools are not toys.

review.q: How do you carry scissors across a room?
choices: Closed, in your fist, point down, walking
review.why: Closed, point down, walking. A trip then cannot hurt anyone.

review.q: How do you hand scissors to a friend?
review.why: Handle first keeps every hand away from the point.

review.q: A knife slips off the counter. Right move?
choices: Step back and let it fall
review.why: Never catch a falling knife. The floor can take the hit.

review.q: Which knife may a kid use on a banana?
review.why: A butter knife is dull and has no point. Sharp knives are for grown-ups.
Broken glass is a grown-up job. Kids tell and stay back.
